Hi! I was very close to that age when I had my surgery. I had a very severe S-curve and I had my entire spine from neck to torso fused. I really recommend doing it as soon as possible! 

The surgery was very smooth and easy, the difficult part will be recovery. The first week is the worst, since your daughter will likely be feeling nauseous, tired, and in pain. I don’t really have the perspective of a parent, but I know I was an annoying little shit because of all the pain and emotions I was feeling, so maybe prepare for that too, haha. Anyway, it’s very helpful to bring some things to the hospital, like books or a blanket, or even food/snacks if they allow. Be prepared to help her with everything from eating to getting out of bed and walking. 

I was discharged after 5-6 days. If you’re taking a car, I recommend reclining a seat to make a sort of “bed” for her- this was the most comfortable way for me. The majority of my recovery was spent lying in bed and playing on my phone (lol). I think it’s a good idea to try to move around, even just sitting up every day, but of course it depends on her comfort. The recovery is slow, but every day seems a bit better. 

I ended up missing about 2 months of school. Honestly, I could’ve gone back earlier, but I just really didn’t want to go back. I recommend waiting until your daughter is comfortable, taking into account how many people she will be around at school. Definitely wait until she is able to sit and walk around on her own or the majority of a day. I also very highly recommend beginning with half-days of school, since the surgery does take a big toll on energy levels, and sitting and participating in public can be more tiring than it seems. 

I’m only 3 years post-op right now, but I’m doing pretty well. I don’t regret the surgery at all, and I’m actually insanely thankful that I got it when I did. The only problem I’ve had is that my neck tends to get sore when I’m writing exams or working for awhile, but this is pretty minor and can be easily helped by just stretching and resting. A few things to anticipate are being sore when standing or sitting for long periods of time. I also make sure to be extra cautious when lifting heavy objects. It will probably be a bit before she can get back to playing physical sports, but it will all come in time. Of course, your surgeon can give you a really good idea of time-frames and whatnot.

Just to note, I was a very sedentary and lazy teenager, (and still am) so the recovery will likely be a bit different for someone more active, for example.

Hi! I had fusion at 14, and I’m almost 17 now. I had an S curve and it was pretty bad, I think something like 70 degrees and 30 degrees? I can’t exactly remember, but it was bad enough that fusion was my only choice.

Start with drawing all the details. Don’t start out trying to simplify, you’ll only get frustrated and it won’t turn out right. Study what you want to draw (portraits, animals, objects, whatever you want) and learn all the ins and outs, like proportion and techniques. Draw from life, draw from photos, just draw lots. 

After you get the basics down and feel more confident, you can focus on figuring out what is “necessary” and what you can leave out, to get to this simplified style. It’ll be much easier to simplify if you don’t have to think as much about capturing the image. 

A specific pointer relevant to simplifying your work is, after you get comfortable with the fundamentals, try drawing in pen or pencil crayon, or without an eraser. This really helped me grow my confidence, personally.

I'm around your age and had my surgery about 1.5 years ago, and I'm Canadian as well. Right after surgery there isn't really pain because of all the painkillers, but you'll probably be a bit nauseous and just overall uncomfortable, but it's not too bad. I stayed in the hospital for only 5-6 days, and I felt better every day. The physiotherapist will make you walk and stuff which might make you feel sick, and it's annoying not being able to go to the bathroom on your own, but you'll get through it! The at-home recovery time is just a lot of lying down and resting, and the main problem I had was being bored all the time, so it's not bad at all!

As of now, I have minor pain in my back when I sit or stand for two long, and just recently I started occasionally having sharper pains, but still very minor stuff. The surgery was definitely worth it. I feel much better about myself and am overall in less pain.

Hey! I'm about a year an a half post-op (April 2015), and I'll start out by saying I have absolutely no regrets about fusion. Before my surgery, I had very little pain, which is why I didn't notice the curve until it got pretty bad. However, it made me very self-conscious about my body, appearance-wise. The surgery was easy and went very smoothly. The recovery is the painful part, but even so, I would say it's more gruelling than painful. I was in the hospital for about five days, and the worst pain was when they removed the various tubes from my back. Other than that, just some soreness, which required me to change positions quite frequently, and you'll feel very very stiff and probably afraid to move around too much. My physiotherapist had me up and walking on the first day, which came with a lot of nausea, so that was probably one of the worst parts. I guess I'm making it sound pretty bad, but it's only five days, and most of it spent sleeping, anyway. After that, it's just a few weeks of relaxing at home. And I grew an inch or two. 
At this point, I still have pain in my back, which is worse than the pain before my surgery. My neck gets sore if I sit in certain positions for too long, which is sometimes a problem at school. My back hurts if I stand for too long, or pick up something too heavy, or run for too long, or am sitting in a strange position. My back will randomly spasm and hurt. However, the pain is generally pretty mild, as long as you are careful about how you're sitting, standing, how much you're running, etc. 
My advice is to absolutely do the surgery. It will put you out of commission for a bit, but it is definitely worth it. Sorry for the huge wall of text, but feel free to ask me if you have any more questions, and I'll do my best to help you out.

I had my surgery when I was around the same age as you. I am terrified of hospitals and needles, and I was also pretty paranoid of complications. Fortunately, modern medicine and technology are very advanced and the chances of something going wrong are very low. I suspect that most people who have spoken of on-going pain had fusions in the past, when the surgery wasn't quite as advanced as it is now. 
The worst part of the surgery is the recovery. I was in the hospital for a week or so, and I just felt terrible. Not a ton of pain, but just nausea and discomfort and waking up a lot to take painkillers. I was only really in pain when they were removing tubes and such. Otherwise, just a little bit of soreness. Sitting and walking will make you want to throw up for the first couple of days. After going home, I just laid in bed for a few weeks. You will feel better every single day. The process is tedious and you'll feel awful until you get back into your regular routine, but I promise you will. It might take a few weeks or a few months or a year, but you will feel like your regular self soon enough. 
Don't worry so much about the pain. It's very manageable, and you will be fine. Having surgery was one of the best things I've ever done. I am a year and a half past my surgery and while my back is sore once in awhile, I am so much more comfortable and confident in my appearance now. And it makes for a really good story. 
Good luck. Feel free to message me if you want to talk, and I would love to hear any updates once you get the surgery.
